prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, trapping neutral atoms at the magic wavelength to reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a single, sharply defined idea with a decisive realization. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removes the Doppler, recoil and lattice light-shift limits, and the demonstrations that followed combined single-ion-like accuracy with the statistics of many atoms. The result is a measurement capability that did not exist before: fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, independent agreement among clocks in several national laboratories, millimetre-to-centimetre-scale tests of gravitational redshift, searches for varying constants and ultralight dark matter, and a credible basis for redefining the second. B030 is also ranked by all eight openings and placed in the top three by six of them, the highest on the shortlist, so the committee already agrees on its standing. The two-name attribution (Katori for the concept and first realizations, Ye for record accuracy, many-body clock physics and comparison technology) is the cleanest on the list, and the work is neither prize-duplicating nor premature. The 2005 prize covered the frequency comb and the 2012 prize covered quantum control of single trapped ions; neither covered a neutral-atom lattice clock.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is partial overlap with earlier metrology recognition (2005 and 2012), together with the unresolved credit boundary toward other lattice-clock contributors (Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow and the Boulder and Tokyo colleagues) and the ion-clock groups. The redefinition of the second has also not happened, so a critic can say the practical culmination is still pending. A further caution is that Ye's accuracy record is partly a refinement of an existing concept, so the committee must be satisfied that the prize honours the invention and its realization rather than a series of performance records.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube (B020) first as an instrument-driven discovery that opened a new observational window, and notes that B030 may be seen as partly duplicating the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes.
responses.response: I accept that IceCube is a genuine discovery, and I do not dismiss it, so I include B020 among the candidates I would not oppose. But I disagree on duplication. The 2005 prize recognised the comb as a ruler and the 2012 prize recognised control of single ions; the lattice clock is a different scheme resting on a different physical idea, the magic wavelength that cancels the trap light shift. Where I share your concern is attribution: Halzen, Karle and Spiering sit on top of AMANDA, Baikal and a large collaboration, and the split between conception, construction and analysis remains unsettled. B030 does not have that problem, which is why I still put it first. I would revisit B020 if a clearer attribution rule for the IceCube leadership emerged from this round.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks Car-Parrinello ab initio molecular dynamics (B022) first on the grounds of unusually clean two-name credit and four decades of use, and ranks B030 low (7), partly because he judges it outside his field and notes the pending SI redefinition.
responses.response: The attribution argument for B022 is the strongest on the list, and I agree it is overdue on maturity. My reservation is about fit rather than quality: the 1985 paper is a method for simulating matter, and the committee will need to decide whether that is a physics discovery or invention in the sense of the will. I do not think it is excluded, but it makes B022 a less secure first choice than a measurement that changed what experiment can resolve. On your point about waiting for the redefinition of the second, I disagree. The criterion is the invention and its consequences, and those are already established through independent clock comparisons at 1e-18; the redefinition is a metrological decision that follows the physics rather than validating it. I would be open to B022 as the second prize part only if the three-person limit permits, which it does not with B030 intact, so I treat B022 as a strong reserve rather than an alternative I am proposing.

responses.point: Lindroth also ranks B030 first, stressing that the underlying atomic physics (light shifts, forbidden transitions, blackbody and many-body shifts) is a clear original idea, and recalls that neither 2005 nor 2012 covered lattice clocks.
responses.response: I agree and want to add the point that matters for attribution. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal is the conceptual invention, but the clock only became a leading instrument because the Boulder effort drove the systematic evaluation to the 1e-18 level and into the many-body regime. Dropping either name would misstate the history. Where I would qualify your recollection is that the 2012 prize covered control of single ions, not clocks as such; ion-clock groups (and Lemonde's and others' lattice-clock work) are therefore a fair counter-argument, and we should say clearly in the citation that the award is for the lattice-clock concept and its realization, not for optical clocks in general.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B030 first and B004 third, and observes that choosing three of four names in B004 necessarily leaves out a key contributor.
responses.response: That is why I rank B030 above B004 even though I respect the cold-atom lattice story. The Hubbard-model proposal by Zoller and collaborators, the Mott transition by Greiner and Bloch, and the fermionic work by Esslinger are each decisive, and Jaksch is not even credited, so any trio is a compromise. I proposed Bloch, Zoller and Esslinger in my opening; I accept that omitting Greiner is arguable, and I would not defend my trio against a trio of Bloch, Greiner and Zoller. Because the credit problem is real, B004 is my first alternative rather than my preference.

uncertainties: How to weigh other lattice-clock groups (Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Bloom, Lemke and others) against the two credited names; I cannot settle this from the supplied text.
Whether the committee will treat the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes as having used up the topic, or accept lattice clocks as a distinct invention.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should delay recognition; I think not, but others may.
For B004, the choice of three among Bloch, Greiner, Zoller and Esslinger, and the absence of Jaksch from the credited names.
statement.conflict_note: I trained in Lund laser spectroscopy and spent a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, which is the scientific lineage from which Jun Ye's group at JILA developed; this is a documented professional connection and should be known when B030 is discussed, although the profile shows no direct collaboration, supervisory or institutional tie to Katori or Ye. I also work in atomic physics and quantum optics, so B004 (including Zoller) lies in a neighbouring community with European quantum-memory and quantum-information collaborations; I know of no specific documented relationship to Bloch, Zoller or Esslinger. No recusal need is apparent from the provided profile, but I flag the field proximity.
